newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech leader puts on brave face before lung surgery.
newsitem.headline: Czech leader puts on brave face before lung surgery.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel headed into exploratory lung surgery next week assuring listeners in his weekly radio address on Sunday that he was in "no serious danger".

Havel, 60, was admitted to hospital last Monday after his office said he was suffering from a case of pneumonia which caused him to curtail his official schedule for the rest of November and early December.
Surgeons at the hospital have described the treatment needed as "medium-serious".

But in his regular weekly address on Czech radio, Havel played down any immediate danger saying the surgery would remove "an unfriendly spot or dot, which has been found in my lungs and whose nature is so far unknown".
"But even if it were to be harmful, it is so small and conveniently situated that I seem to be in no serious danger," he added saying he had not felt better in weeks.
In a sign that Havel was still in fighting spirit, he sharply criticised a local private television station, TV Nova, for crawling on roofs opposite the hospital to film him through a window.
He said he expected "a minimal amount of good taste" from the station.

Havel, a former dissident playwright who was one of the leaders of Prague's 1989 revolution over the Communist government, is known to be a heavy smoker, but the illness has not been officially linked to his smoking.
The illness comes just as a sensitive post-World War Two reconciliation treaty with Germany, on which Havel has spent much effort, nears its completion.
The treaty is to address the Nazi occupation of Bohemia and Moravia, and the subsequent expulsion of ethnic Germans after the Czech lands were liberated in 1945.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said recently that he hoped the treaty could be signed before by the year's end, and Czech politicians have been quoted in local media saying they expected a possible signing of the agreement in mid-December.
The president's office has not commented on how his illness might affect the treaty.

Havel has had various ailments, none considered serious, during his nearly seven years as president of Czechoslovakia and the independent Czech Republic after a peaceful split with Slovakia at the beginning of 1993.
He had urgent surgery last February after a polyp in his mouth started bleeding, but that incident was not considered serious.
Last January, Havel's wife Olga died of complications, reported to have stemmed from uterine cancer.
